title: The Decision Geometry of Covariance Estimation for the Global Minimum-Variance Portfolio under Heavy Tails

p.t: Risk-based portfolio construction begins with an estimate of the covariance matrix of asset returns, and the global minimum-variance portfolio (GMVP) is its purest instance: it depends on the covariance matrix alone, with no expected-return input, and so isolates the question of how covariance-estimation quality translates into portfolio quality. That question is sharpened by a mismatch between what is estimated and what is measured. The estimation literature evaluates covariance estimators by matrix-norm loss-operator, Frobenius, or spectral-and a mature theory characterises minimax rates for these losses, including dimension-free guarantees under heavy tails and adversarial corruption (Abdalla and Zhivotovskiy 2022) and robust estimators for heavy-tailed data (Ke et al. 2019). But matrix-norm loss is not the quantity the investor experiences. The investor experiences regret: the excess variance of the portfolio formed from the estimate relative to the portfolio formed from the truth. A covariance estimator can be poor in matrix norm yet induce small regret, or accurate in matrix norm yet induce large regret, depending on which directions of the matrix it gets wrong relative to the portfolio's exposures. The central question of this paper is the exact relationship between covariance-estimation error and GMVP regret-which directions of error the decision is exposed to, and how strongly. Decision-focused learning (DFL) has recently been applied to exactly this gap, training covariance models to optimise downstream decision quality rather than predictive error (Kim et al. 2025;Lee et al. 2024). These works demonstrate empirically that decision-aware estimation can outperform error-minimising estimation for the GMVP, but they are learning-based and offer no characterisation of why, nor any consistency or rate theory: they optimise against an oracle covariance and report outof-sample performance. This paper supplies the missing structure. We give the exact decision geometry-which directions of covariance error the GMVP decision actually sees-and the consistency theory under heavy tails.

1. Exact regret identity and non-asymptotic bound (Theorem 4.2). For the GMVP, regret equals ( w -w) ⊤ Σ( w -w) exactly, and is bounded by C 0 ∥w∥ 2 ∥E∥ 2 2 cond(Σ) with E = Σ -Σ and C 0 an absolute constant. The bound scales with portfolio concentration ∥w∥ 2 and the conditioning of the truth, not with full matrix-norm accuracy. 2. The (p -1)-dimensional decision geometry (Proposition 5.1). GMVP regret depends on the p 2 -entry error matrix E only through the (p -1) components of Ew orthogonal to 1. Equivalently, regret is invariant to every error E with Ew ∥ 1; invariance to the scale direction E = cΣ is an exact special case. This is the precise sense in which the decision ignores most of the covariance error. 3. Heavy-tail application (Section 6). For returns with tail index κ ∈ (2, 4), the centred covariance estimator converges in operator norm at n -(κ-2)/κ and GMVP regret at n -2(κ-2)/κ via Theorem 4.2. The decision-focused gain is a constant and a concentration discount, not a rate improvement; we state this plainly and report a high-conditioning boundary of the rate prediction. 4. Pre-registered confirmation (Section 7). A skew-t/t-copula design with a committed statistical analysis plan confirms the identity, the geometry (to machine precision across dimension), and the rates, with an honest account of where finite-sample and high-conditioning effects bind.

Organisation. Section 3 fixes notation and defines the regret object. Section 4 proves the exact regret identity and the non-asymptotic bound. Section 5 establishes the (p -1)-dimensional decision geometry. Section 6 applies the framework to heavytailed returns and states the regret rate with its high-conditioning boundary. Section 7 reports the pre-registered confirmation. Section 8 relates the results to prior work and states their limitations, and Section 9 concludes. 2 Background and related work Our results connect three lines of research that have largely developed in parallel: the statistical theory of covariance estimation, the long literature on estimation error in mean-variance portfolios, and the recent decision-focused learning programme. We review each in turn, with emphasis on the precise point at which our contribution enters.

p.s: Covariance estimation under a matrix-norm loss
p.t: The dominant paradigm for evaluating a covariance estimator Σ is the loss ∥ Σ-Σ∥ in a matrix norm-operator, Frobenius, or spectral. In the large-dimensional regime where the dimension p is comparable to the sample size n, the sample covariance matrix is inconsistent in operator norm and ill-conditioned: its eigenvalues are over-dispersed relative to the truth (Marčenko and Pastur 1967), which is precisely what corrupts any portfolio formed by inverting it. Two broad responses have emerged. The first is shrinkage: Ledoit and Wolf (2004) introduced the asymptotically optimal linear combination of the sample covariance with a scaled identity, a well-conditioned and distributionfree estimator, later extended to constant-correlation targets (Ledoit and Wolf 2003), nonlinear (eigenvalue) shrinkage (Ledoit and Wolf 2012), and oracle-approximating forms (Chen et al. 2010); the idea traces to the empirical-Bayes estimator of Haff (1980). Recent work has begun to question whether minimising a matrix-norm loss is even the right target for portfolio construction: Bongiorno and Challet (2023) show that nonlinear shrinkage optimised for estimation accuracy can be far from optimal for portfolio variance, a finding that directly motivates the decision-focused viewpoint we formalise. The second is structured estimation under sparsity or factor assumptions, with minimax rates established in operator and Frobenius norm (Bickel and Levina 2008;Cai et al. 2010;Lam and Fan 2009;El Karoui 2008;Lounici 2014). A more recent strand seeks dimension-free and heavy-tail-robust guarantees. Koltchinskii and Lounici (2017) obtained operator-norm bounds scaling with the effective rank r(Σ) = tr(Σ)/∥Σ∥ rather than the ambient dimension; Ke et al. (2019) gave user-friendly heavy-tailed estimators; and Mendelson and Zhivotovskiy (2020) and Abdalla and Zhivotovskiy (2022) established sub-Gaussian-type operator-norm rates under only low-order moment assumptions, the latter achieving the optimal dimensionfree rate ∥Σ∥ r(Σ)/n + κ(p) 2 η 1-2/p under L p -L 2 norm equivalence with p > 4 and adversarial corruption level η. A theme of this literature, made explicit by the classical Bai-Yin theorem (Bai and Yin 1993) and revisited by Tikhomirov (2018) and Abdalla and Zhivotovskiy (2022), is that the regime of fewer than four moments is genuinely harder: below p = 4 the standard p/n-type convergence can fail, and dimension-free rates in this regime remain delicate. Our heavy-tail application (Section 6) operates squarely in this sub-four-moment regime, κ ∈ (2, 4), which is one reason the regret rate we obtain is governed by the heavy-tailed-mean exponent rather than a Bai-Yin rate.

p.s: Covariance estimation under a matrix-norm loss
p.t: The unifying feature of all of the above is that accuracy is measured in a matrix norm, chosen for analytical tractability and generality. None of these losses is the quantity a portfolio actually pays. Our Theorem 4.2 is the bridge: it converts any operator-norm guarantee from this literature into a GMVP regret guarantee, and shows that the conversion is mediated by portfolio-specific quantities that can be far smaller than the matrix-norm error itself.

That optimised portfolios are acutely sensitive to estimation error has been understood since Markowitz (1952). Michaud (1989) called mean-variance optimisation an "error-maximiser"; Chopra and Ziemba (1993) quantified the relative damage from errors in means versus covariances, and Best and Grauer (1991) and Klein and Bawa (1976) analysed the sensitivity of the optimal portfolio to its inputs. A central finding of this literature is that errors in expected returns are far more damaging than errors in covariances, and that expected returns are notoriously hard to estimate (Merton 1980), which motivates the study of the global minimum-variance portfolio (GMVP): depending on no expected-return input, it isolates the covariance-estimation problem (Jagannathan and Ma 2003;DeMiguel et al. 2009). The GMVP has accordingly become the canonical testbed for covariance-estimation quality, and a substantial body of work studies its estimation directly-through constrained or shrunk weights (Jagannathan and Ma 2003), high-dimensional and Bayesian estimators of the GMVP itself (Bodnar et al. 2018(Bodnar et al. , 2017;;Frahm and Memmel 2010), and the empirical performance of minimum-variance investing (Clarke et al. 2011). Kan and Zhou (2007) give an analytical treatment of portfolio choice under parameter uncertainty. Famously, DeMiguel et al. (2009) found that many sophisticated rules fail to beat the naive 1/N portfolio out of sample, underscoring how severely estimation error erodes theoretical optimality. This literature quantifies how much regret estimation error induces, often through the variance of plug-in weights or out-of-sample performance studies. What it has not provided is an exact and structural account of which directions of covariance error the GMVP decision is sensitive to. Theorem 4.2 and Proposition 5.1 fill that gap: the regret is an exact quadratic in the weight displacement, and the displacement responds to only a (p -1)-dimensional projection of the error.

A recent and rapidly growing programme argues that when an estimate feeds a downstream optimisation, the estimator should be trained to optimise decision quality rather than predictive accuracy. This decision-focused (or end-to-end, or "predictthen-optimize") learning has been developed through differentiable optimisation layers (Amos and Kolter 2017;Agrawal et al. 2019), the "smart predict-then-optimize" loss (Elmachtoub and Grigas 2022), task-based learning (Donti et al. 2017), and melding of the data-decision pipeline (Wilder et al. 2019); see Mandi et al. (2024) for a survey. In portfolio optimisation specifically, decision-focused and end-to-end methods have been applied to mean-variance construction (Butler and Kwon 2023;Costa and Iyengar 2023;Anis and Kwon 2025). Two contributions are directly adjacent to ours. Lee et al. (2024) analyse how decision-focused training reshapes a return prediction model for mean-variance optimisation, showing that the decision gradient tilts the mean-squared prediction error by the inverse covariance Σ -1 , inducing systematic "strategic biases" that improve portfolio decisions despite larger prediction error. Their object is the expected-return vector, not the covariance, and their analysis is of the gradient that drives learning. Most closely related, Kim et al. (2025) apply decision-focused learning to covariance estimation for the GMVP-to our knowledge the first to do so. They derive the decision gradient ∂w * /∂ Σ in closed form and analyse the singular vectors of this gradient, identifying directions (spanned by w ⊗ w and w ⊗ Σ -1 w) that are invariant under the optimisation map, in order to motivate and interpret a learned estimator; they demonstrate empirically that the resulting estimator outperforms shrinkage and prediction-focused baselines in out-of-sample volatility.

Our work is complementary to Kim et al. (2025) and sharpens the theoretical picture in three ways. First, where they characterise invariant singular directions of the decision gradient under a non-trivial-kernel assumption that they note may fail in practice, we prove an exact, assumption-free regret identity (Theorem 4.2) and an exact characterisation of the full (p -1)-dimensional subspace of covariance errors to which GMVP regret is blind (Proposition 5.1). Second, we provide a nonasymptotic regret bound in terms of interpretable quantities-portfolio concentration ∥w∥ 2 and the conditioning of the truth-that no prior decision-focused work supplies. Third, we establish consistency and convergence rates under heavy tails, giving the statistical theory that the empirical decision-focused literature has so far lacked. In short, the decision-focused programme has demonstrated that decision-aware covariance estimation helps; our results explain, exactly and generator-free, why and by how much.

The bound of Theorem 4.2 is generator-free: it converts any operator-norm guarantee on Σ into a regret guarantee, with the conversion mediated by the decision-specific factors ∥w∥ 2 2 and cond(Σ). We now instantiate it in the regime where covariance estimation is most delicate-returns with a finite variance but an infinite fourth moment-and state the regret rate that follows, together with the boundary of that rate that our pre-registered experiments reveal.

We model returns with skew-t marginals coupled by a t-copula, a design that separately controls tail heaviness, asymmetry, and dependence geometry. Let W ∼ χ 2 ν /ν be a common mixing variable with ν = κ ∈ (2, 4) the tail index, let Z ∼ N (0, R) with R a correlation matrix, and set T = Z/ √ W (a multivariate-t vector). The observed return on asset i is the skew transform with skewness parameter α (we use α = 5). The marginal tail index of X i is κ; the fourth moment is infinite for κ < 4, so classical fourth-moment-based covariance theory does not apply. A prerequisite for any rate statement is an exact population target. The closed-form covariance of ( 6) is, writing m where ρ ij = R ij . Comparing a non-centred estimator against the centred target ( 7)-( 8) produces an artificial bias floor that can be mistaken for non-convergence of the estimator under heavy tails. All results below use the centred estimator; the distinction is material precisely because the marginals are skewed.

Proposition 6.1 (Heavy-tail regret rate) For the centred sample covariance under the model of Section 6.1 with tail index κ ∈ (2, 4), and consequently, by Theorem 4.2, Proof sketch The entries of Σ -Σ are sample means of products X i X j centred at their expectation. Under the scale-mixture (6) the heavy behaviour enters through the common factor 1/W , whose square 1/W 2 has tail index κ/2 ∈ (1, 2); hence the entrywise fluctuations are heavy-tailed sums with infinite variance, for which the sample-mean deviation is of order n -(κ-2)/κ (the heavy-tailed-mean rate for a summand with tail index κ/2; see Vershynin (2018) for the relevant concentration tools). The operator norm of a fixed-dimensional matrix is equivalent to its entrywise norm up to constants, giving (10). Substituting (10) into the bound (5) of Theorem 4.2, and noting that ∥w∥ 2 2 and cond(Σ) are fixed constants in n, yields R( Σ) = O P (n -2(κ-2)/κ ). A formal statement requires a uniform-integrability condition on the centred products; we provide the rate at the level of the verified simulation and leave the sharp regularity hypotheses to future work.

The factor of two in (11) relative to ( 10) is the squared propagation implied by the exact identity (3): regret is a quadratic in the weight displacement, which is in turn linear in the estimation error, so the regret exponent is twice the operator-norm exponent. This is confirmed directly: across κ ∈ {2.5, 3, 3.5, 5} at moderate conditioning, the ratio of the log-mean regret slope to the log-mean displacement slope lies in [1.85, 1.99] (supplementary battery3 centered results; the median-based ratio is closer to 2.0 throughout). Remark 4 (The decision-focused gain is a constant, not a rate) We emphasise what (11) does and does not claim. The regret converges at twice the operator-norm exponent, but the operator norm does converge-there is no rate decoupling between matrix estimation and decision quality. The advantage of the decision-focused viewpoint is the constant in the bound: regret scales with ∥w∥ 2 2 cond(Σ) rather than with full matrix-norm accuracy, and is exactly invariant to the (p -1)-codimensional blind subspace of Proposition 5.1. This is a sharper constant and a concentration discount, not a faster rate. We state this plainly to forestall the stronger and incorrect reading that decision-focused estimation is consistent where matrix estimation is not.

p.s: A boundary of the rate prediction
p.t: The rate (10) is the heavy-tailed-mean rate derived under moderate conditioning, and it is confirmed cleanly there: at cond(Σ) = 1, every κ matches its prediction to within the pre-registered tolerance, with operator-norm slopes of -0.194, -0.315, -0.381, -0.476 against predictions -0.20, -0.333, -0.429, -0.50 for κ = 2.5, 3, 3.5, 5 respectively, and displacement slopes tracking these (supplementary battery3 centered results). At high conditioning the prediction is a slight over-estimate of convergence speed for intermediate tail index. With the generator correctly coloured to the target covariance (so that Σ converges to the same Σ used as truth-a self-check we verify cell by cell), the corrected cond(Σ) = 5 cells match the prediction for κ ∈ {2.5, 3, 5} (displacement slopes -0.179, -0.306, -0.461 against -0.20, -0.333, -0.50) but fall slightly short at κ = 3.5: the measured displacement slope is -0.363 against the predicted -0.429 (supplementary battery3b cond5 results). Extending the sample ladder to n = 10 6 does not close the gap-the slope on the upper ladder is -0.376 and on the top decade -0.318, rather than steepening toward -0.429 (supplementary resolve k35 cond5). We therefore report this as a genuine boundary rather than a finite-sample artefact: at high conditioning and intermediate tail index, the effective convergence rate of the regret-relevant error is somewhat slower than n -(κ-2)/κ . The squared-propagation relationship is nonetheless preserved at this cell (regret-todisplacement slope ratio 1.94), so the structural content of Theorem 4.2 is intact; it is the absolute operator-norm rate, at high conditioning, that the clean prediction slightly overstates. We prefer to record the measured rates and this boundary rather than the idealisation alone.

We confirm the results on the generative model of Section 6.1 under a committed analysis plan: the design, the sample-size ladder, the per-claim pass criteria, and the summary statistic were fixed in writing before the confirmation run. The simulation code, the analysis plan, and the raw outputs are provided as supplementary material; all generators are seeded for bit-for-bit reproducibility, and every covariance estimate is centred (Remark 3). We report three groups of claims, in the order a reader reproducing the work would run them: the exact geometry, the rates, and the high-conditioning boundary.

Throughout, p is the number of assets, α = 5 the skew parameter, and κ ∈ {2.5, 3, 3.5, 5} the tail index; the true correlation R has condition number cond(R) ∈ {1, 5}. Rates are estimated by ordinary least squares of the log of a summary statistic against log n on the ladder n ∈ {10 3 , 4×10 3 , 1.6×10 4 , 6.4×10 4 , 2.56×10 5 } with 200 replicates per cell, and reported with a 5,000-draw bootstrap confidence interval. The summary statistic for rate claims is the log-mean (geometric mean) across replicates; for a quadratic of a heavy-tailed quantity the upper sample quantiles are themselves heavy and converge at their own rate, so the geometric mean is the appropriate location statistic for an exponent, with the median reported alongside. A pre-run self-check requires the centred estimator to converge to the closed-form target (7)-( 8) before any rate is fitted; at κ = 3, n = 6.4×10 4 the centred sample diagonal is 1.805 ± 0.167 against the closed-form 1.831, while the non-centred diagonal is 2.973 ± 0.171, confirming both that centring is applied and that omitting it would inject the O(1) bias of Remark 3.

Extending the ladder to n = 10 6 does not close the gap-the upper-decade slope is -0.318 rather than steepening toward -0.429-so this is a genuine boundary of the rate prediction at high conditioning and intermediate tail index, not a finite-sample transient (Section 6.3). The exact identity, the (p -1) decision geometry, and the scale invariance hold to machine precision and independently of dimension. The heavy-tail rates hold at moderate conditioning across the tail-index range, with the squared propagation confirmed throughout. The single departure is a slightly shallow operator-norm exponent at high conditioning and intermediate tail index, which we report rather than suppress. None of the confirmed claims depends on the decision and the covariance estimator decoupling in rate; consistent with Remark 4, the decision-focused content is the exact geometry and the concentration-scaled constant, both of which the experiments bear out.

A mature theory establishes minimax rates for estimating Σ in operator, Frobenius, and spectral norm, including dimension-free guarantees under heavy tails and adversarial corruption (Abdalla and Zhivotovskiy 2022) and user-friendly robust estimators for heavy-tailed data (Ke et al. 2019). That theory takes a matrix-norm loss as primitive. Our contribution is orthogonal to it rather than competing: Theorem 4.2 shows how any operator-norm guarantee converts into a GMVP regret guarantee, and Proposition 5.1 shows that the conversion discards most of the matrix through a (p -1)-dimensional projection. We use the heavy-tailed operator-norm rate as an input (Proposition 6.1); we do not improve it. The value added is to identify which part of that error the decision is exposed to, and by how much (∥w∥ 2 2 cond(Σ) rather than the full matrix-norm accuracy). Decision-focused learning. A recent line trains covariance or return models to optimise downstream decision quality rather than predictive error. Kim et al. (2025) learn a covariance model specifically for the GMVP and report out-of-sample gains over error-minimising estimation; Lee et al. (2024) document, for the mean-variance problem, that decision-focused training induces "strategic biases" that improve portfolios despite larger prediction error. These works are empirical and learning-based: they optimise against an oracle covariance and demonstrate that decision-aware estimation can help, but they do not characterise why, nor establish consistency or rates. Our results supply exactly that missing structure. Proposition 5.1 explains, as an exact identity, why decision-aware estimation can ignore most of the covariance error: the GMVP decision depends on the error only through a (p -1)-dimensional projection of its action on the weights, so an estimator that is inaccurate in the complementary directions pays nothing. The "strategic biases" that Lee et al. (2024) observe empirically are, from this viewpoint, the estimator declining to spend capacity on directions the decision does not see. We thus complement the decision-focused learning programme with the geometry and the consistency theory it has so far lacked.

A separate tradition estimates the portfolio weights or the precision-matrix action directly, rather than estimating Σ and inverting, on the grounds that the weights are the object of interest and have fewer effective degrees of freedom. Our analysis gives this intuition an exact form: the regret-relevant content of the covariance error is the (p -1)-dimensional vector P 1 Ew, so the decision genuinely lives in a lower-dimensional object than the 1 2 p(p + 1)-parameter matrix. We caution, however, against over-reading this as a dimension-rate reduction: the relevant subspace still grows with p, and the convergence rate of the decision error inherits that of the matrix error in the directions that matter (Remark 4). More broadly, the gap between a conventionally reported accuracy metric and the quantity that actually governs outcomes recurs across performance evaluation: in the backtesting context, for instance, two return streams can share an identical Sharpe ratio yet deliver sharply different lived experience (Fonseca 2026). The present analysis is the covariance-estimation instance of the same principle-operator-norm accuracy is not the quantity the portfolio pays.

For a practitioner implementing a minimum-variance or risk-parity allocator, the results translate into concrete guidance. What to optimise. The quantity that governs out-of-sample portfolio variance is not the matrix-norm accuracy of the covariance estimate but the regret ( w -w) ⊤ Σ( w -w), which Theorem 4.2 bounds by ∥w∥ 2 ∥E∥ 2 2 cond(Σ) up to an absolute constant. A modelselection or hyperparameter-tuning loop that scores candidate estimators by Frobenius or operator error is therefore optimising the wrong objective; it should score them by realised portfolio variance, or by a regret proxy, instead. This is consistent with the empirical finding of Bongiorno and Challet (2023) that estimators tuned for matrix accuracy can be far from optimal for the portfolio, and it gives that finding an exact explanation. Where to spend capacity. Proposition 5.1 shows the decision sees the error only through P 1 Ew, a (p -1)-dimensional projection: error in the directions the portfolio does not load on is free, and error aligned with the current holdings is what is paid for. A data-limited practitioner should accordingly concentrate estimation effort-more data, stronger priors, tighter shrinkage-on the covariance structure among the assets the portfolio actually weights, rather than spreading it uniformly across all 1 2 p(p + 1) matrix entries. What raises the stakes. The bound makes the two danger signals explicit and monitorable: a concentrated portfolio (large ∥w∥ 2 -a few large positions hurt more than many small ones) and an ill-conditioned covariance (large cond(Σ)-some combinations of assets far less volatile than others) both amplify the cost of a given estimation error, so an implementer can track these two scalars as a live risk diagnostic and respond with weight constraints or conditioning control when they spike.

Three boundaries of the contribution should be stated plainly. First, the decision-focused advantage we establish is a sharper constant and a concentration discount, not a faster rate: under correct centring the covariance estimator converges, and regret converges at twice its exponent, with no rate decoupling (Remark 4). Second, the geometry is specific to the GMVP decision; the unconstrained varianceminimising portfolio is what makes Σw proportional to 1 and the linear term vanish exactly. Extending the exact identity to mean-variance portfolios with a return term, or to constrained portfolios, is left to future work, though the bound of Theorem 4.2 should admit analogues. Third, the heavy-tail rate prediction is slightly optimistic at high conditioning and intermediate tail index, a boundary we document rather than suppress (Section 6.3). None of these qualifications touches the exact algebraic results, which hold to machine precision and independently of dimension.

We have characterised exactly how covariance-estimation error maps into suboptimality of the global minimum-variance portfolio. The regret is an exact quadratic in the weight displacement (Theorem 4.2), bounded non-asymptotically by ∥w∥ 2 2 ∥E∥ 2 2 cond(Σ), so the decision is exposed to estimation error only through portfolio concentration and the conditioning of the truth, not through matrix-norm accuracy as such. The decision sees, moreover, only a (p -1)-dimensional projection of the p 2entry error matrix (Proposition 5.1): it is exactly invariant to a codimension-(p -1) subspace of covariance errors, of which scale invariance is the single special case usually noted informally. Applied to heavy-tailed returns, this yields a regret rate of n -2(κ-2)/κ for tail index κ ∈ (2, 4), twice the centred operator-norm exponent, confirmed under a pre-registered analysis plan together with an honestly reported boundary at high conditioning. The practical reading is that decision-focused covariance estimation, which has been pursued empirically, has an exact and simple geometric basis: the global minimum-variance decision is blind to most of the covariance error, and an estimator does well to spend its statistical budget on the directions the decision actually sees. The advantage this confers is a constant and a concentration discount rather than a faster rate-a more modest but more defensible claim than rate decoupling. Natural extensions are to mean-variance and constrained portfolios, where the exact identity will require modification but the bound should carry over, and to estimators that exploit the (p -1)-dimensional geometry directly.
